content.text: {"grade": 6, "complete": false, "main_gap": "The proof that at least one non-unit always remains rests on a false general principle (a non-increasing positive integer sequence 'can never reach 0'); the true reason (a move needs two non-units and yields at least one) is not given.", "errors": [{"description": "Invalid justification that K \u2265 1 always. A non-increasing positive integer can certainly reach 0. The correct argument (each move requires two non-units and produces lcm(m,n)>1, so K drops by at most 1 and moves stop at K=1; or G_p \u2265 1 for a prime dividing A_1) is missing, though easily supplied.", "quote": "A nonnegative integer that\nnever increases and starts at a positive value can never reach \\(0\\); hence \\(K\\ge1\\) at\nevery stage"}], "notes": "Termination via lexicographic (P,K) descent and the prime-wise Euclidean gcd invariant are both correct and well presented; the closed form M = \u220f p^{gcd of valuations} is right. Only the non-vanishing-of-K step is unsound but trivially repairable."}
